misconception.description: computing payback from accounting profit rather than from cash flow, which deducts depreciation and so counts the cost of the asset twice

worked_example.text: A laundry buys a EUR 45,000 machine that brings in EUR 15,000 of cash a year. Depreciated over five years, it is charged EUR 9,000 a year, so the accounts report a profit of EUR 6,000.
worked_example.solution: Payback = 45,000 / 15,000 = 3.00 years. Using the reported profit would give 45,000 / 6,000 = 7.50 years, far too long, because the depreciation has been deducted from a return that never actually paid it.

problem.text: A hotel invests EUR 84,000 in a new kitchen with a seven-year life. The kitchen is expected to bring in EUR 24,000 of cash a year. Depreciation of EUR 10,000 a year is charged against it, so the accounts report an annual profit of EUR 14,000. What is the payback period?

distractors.note: the documented misconception: the accounting profit used in place of cash flow
dividing by the cash of the whole life rather than one year of it

hints: Payback asks how long the money put in takes to come back, so both halves of the division have to be measured in cash.
Two of the figures describe the same year. One is the cash the kitchen brings in; the other is what the accounts report after a depreciation charge that nobody actually pays out.
Divide the amount invested by the annual cash flow and give the answer in years.
worked_solution: Step 1: pick the cash figure. The kitchen brings in EUR 24,000 a year; the EUR 14,000 is that same cash after a EUR 10,000 bookkeeping charge, and no money leaves the hotel for depreciation. Step 2: divide the investment by the annual cash flow: 84,000 / 24,000 = 3.50 years. The hotel has its money back halfway through the fourth year. Using the profit figure would give 84,000 / 14,000 = 6.00 years, almost twice as long, because the purchase price is already in the numerator and the depreciation charges it a second time.

near_transfer.text: A second kitchen also costs EUR 84,000 but its cash flows are uneven: EUR 20,000 in year 1, EUR 28,000 in year 2 and EUR 40,000 in year 3. What is its payback period?

distractors.note: assuming every year repeats the first year's cash flow
assuming every year matches the best year

far_transfer.text: A company approves projects only if they pay back within two and a half years. A proposed machine costs EUR 90,000 and would be depreciated by EUR 15,000 a year. What is the minimum annual cash flow it must generate to be approved?

distractors.note: the misconception: depreciation deducted from the cash the project must produce
multiplying by the limit instead of dividing by it
